publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.

articleTitle: The negotiating agent model for rapid feature development
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: Feature interactions provide one of the most difficult problems in the enhancement of telecommunication systems The authors propose a model for negotiation to resolve conflicts in telecommunications systems at run-time, especially those arising from feature interactions. They describe the model and how it is being implemented as one version of the desktop multi-media conferencing system Touring Machine.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The Touring Machine project: toward a public network platform for multimedia applications
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The Touring Machine project is a research experiment that explores the role of public communications networks in facilitating future multimedia applications. The research focuses on the design and realization of a robust software control infrastructure that enables a broad class of communications applications. The author provides an overview of the Touring Machine project and discusses the second iteration of system design, which currently provides multimedia, desktop communications applications for several dozen researchers at two Bellcore locations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Formal specification-a key to service interactions analysis
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: A demonstration is given of the use of formal specification to analyse service interaction between the CW service (call-waiting) and the CFB service (call-forwarding-busy). In particular, the interaction identified agrees with T.F. Bowen el al. (1989) informal observation. Informal analysis may suffice for simple services but for complex services, the precision of formal specifications is essential. The problem of specifying a large specification with many services is mitigated by limiting the analysis to shared data. Further enhancement can be made through automation which requires specifications to be written in formal language. Some of the automation techniques are: symbolic execution, theorem provers and prototyping systems. Z and Object-Z are ideal for specifying services as they provided a rich set of mathematical objects e.g. sets, functions, sequences etc. for modelling services. Furthermore Z and Object-Z specifications can be prototyped in Prolog, e.g. a Z operation can be converted to Y.-J. Lin's (1990), Prolog state-translation predicates.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Implementing a functional language for highly parallel real time applications
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: This paper describes a fast, highly portable implementation of the real time, symbolic, declarative programming language Erlang. Erlang has been used by Ericsson for prototyping switching systems and tens of thousands of lines of Erlang code have been written. Projects in which Erlang has been used have demonstrated at least an order of magnitude reduction in the work load of the specification-programming-testing cycle when compared to projects using conventional technology. This paper describes some of the implementation techniques used in a fast and highly portable implementation of Erlang. The authors present measurements of the execution speed of Erlang when used to implement a prototype control system for a PABX.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Definition of requirements for a safety critical communications system
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: This paper reports on a feasibility and formal design study carried out for a safety critical communications system. It highlights some important conclusions regarding the requirements definition process for safety critical systems and the role of formal methods within that process. The study applied novel formal approaches to system analysis and design in a practical application in order to gain an understanding of the technical and methodological issues surrounding their use. The paper concentrates on a few of the issues which were highlighted by the study. It starts by explaining the background to the development in terms of the expected role of formal methods within the requirements definition process, the target application and the anticipated nature of the system solutions. Next, issues arising in the various stages of the process are discussed and some of the problems encountered are highlighted. These impacted partly upon the conduct of the development and partly upon the technical solutions themselves. Finally, some of the conclusions from the study are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Performance and functional prototyping from software descriptions
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The use of formal description techniques, in particular standardised, are a prerequisite for transformation of the descriptions into other representations. These can be either a step in the development process or a way to analyse or dimensioning the qualities of the system at an early stage. The paper formulates a general (independent of description technique) methodology for performance analysis at an early stage. It is pointed out that as a side effect it is possible to do functional analysis in a real time model as well. The author presents some results in transforming SDL system specifications into SDL descriptions describing the original SDL system from a performance viewpoint. SDL (specification and description language) has been standardised by CCITT as a suitable description technique for telecommunication systems. The methodology is independent of description technique, and SDL has only been chosen as a suitable example based on experience and available tools.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An object oriented approach for structuring ISDN call processing software
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: In 1989 a pilot project was started at Siemens to gain experience concerning the applicability of object oriented techniques (OOT) in the field of switching system software. In this pilot project an ISDN prototype switch was implemented applying both the principles of object oriented design and the programming language Object-CHILL, an object oriented extension of CHILL. The authors deal with the results reached so far within this project. In this context three subjects are considered in more detail: the influence of OOT on the software development process, the resulting structure of the ISDN call processing software and the impact of OOT on the tool set. In general many of the advantages claimed to be associated with object orientation in other application fields could be confirmed for switching system software.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The CCITT data oriented human-machine interface specification technique
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: International Telegraph and Telephone Consultative Committee (CCITT) is developing draft recommendations on a data oriented human-machine interface specification technique. Draft recommendation text exists on the following topics: approach; reference model; method; data design; formalism; documentation; example documentation; handling of time; explanation and usage of the formalism; requirements of the formalism; and relationships between the HMI and TMN reference models. Also, early attempts have been made to apply the specification technique to the following application areas: alarm surveillance; traffic administration; and access control administration. This paper puts the proposed specification technique into a theoretical perspective for application designers and developers of specification techniques.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Satellites in the corporate network
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: A discussion is given on the issues arising from the management problems of incorporating satellites into corporate networks. Specifically, the following areas are addressed: the part that satellites have to play in corporate networks, and how they are to be managed; the relevance of management standards, with reference to the OSI and the corresponding CCITT standards; and the development of suitable network management workstations, including and idealised architecture.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: TMN information modelling and retrieval by an advanced human-machine interface
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The paper presents the research activities and results in the area of intelligent human machine interface (HMI) for the telecommunication management network (TMN) carried out jointly by CSELT and SIP. The requirements for effective TMN HMI are outlined. The principles used to retrieve information for the operating systems (OSs) are described. The authors also describe a presentation tailored to user's characteristics and role, based on user-friendly graphic dialogue, following the direct manipulation approach.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: CAPE: computer aid for protocol engineering
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: Protocols for telecommunication networks and computer networks are key-elements. A protocol engineering workstation can support the developer to specify, implement and test these protocols. The PROCONSUL (protocol consultant) system developed in Hungary contains a user interface module, several protocol specification modules, conformance testing, simulation and implementation modules and libraries. For large-scale systems, diverse customer needs must be communicated and translated into precise implementations that are consistent with the existing system. The front end of the software development process-from analysis of customer requirements to high level design-is generally time consuming and labour intensive. This paper discusses a CAPE (computer aid for protocol engineering) technology developed for protocol engineering.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rule descriptions for telecommunication services and their transformation into standardized specification descriptions
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: As telecommunication software has become more complex and sophisticated, designers have been obliged to devote considerable time and effort to software development. Specification description technique is an important approach for improving software productivity. However, to achieve high productivity, design support in early stages of software development is even more important. The authors describe a specification method, STR (state transition rule) method, and its verification method. The method allows them to specify and verify service behaviour in the early stages of software development. This paper discusses the transformation of STR descriptions into standardized specification descriptions, such as SDL (functional specification description language). The transformation assumes a certain software architecture and generates interactions among terminals.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Service creation environment for the intelligent network
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: An advanced service creation environment is necessary in the intelligent network to quickly provide services for user's needs. The authors propose a SCE system structure for nonexpert users of telecommunication software that allows customers to develop service logic. To describe and verify service specifications in the high level specification description language is possible using the prototype system. For the future, more advanced and user-friendly services based on broadband ISDN are expected. For these enhancements, service creation environment will play an important role.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Adapting management of DX 200 switching system into TMN object model
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The work for developing standards for TMN (Telecommunications Management Network) has reached a point where the overall principles have been defined and widely accepted. A digital exchange can be considered as network element (NE) in the TMN model. However, the distributed structure, the large amount of software and the wide variety of functionality that are characteristic of many digital exchanges mean that there is an exceptionally large amount of management information within a single NE. DX200 is a digital switching system with a wide variety of applications in public switched network as well as in mobile networks (GSM, NMT). The decentralized architecture DX200 system is based on loosely coupled microcomputers. The demands for modifications in the DX200 system indicated by the TMN object-oriented model are studied and possible solutions to fulfil the new requirements are described. Emphasis is put on studying how the existing management software could be utilized to minimize the amount of work needed to fulfil the requirements suggested by the TMN object-oriented model. The new software architecture must also be flexible enough to allow quick implementation of unknown object classes that are to be defined in international standardization bodies.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Object-oriented system programming for switching systems
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The development of switching systems is time and cost consuming. A report is given on a project within the SIEMENS Corporation where object-oriented techniques were used to develop a switching system for broadband ISDN. Some important components of system software and how their support for object-orientation should look like are discussed. One of these is an operating system that acts as an runtime system for object-oriented features. The effects of this support are shown by some typical applications for switching systems. Another system component is an analysis tool offering a novel type of object-specific trace mechanism. As an introduction to the topic the most important object-oriented terms are defined. The particular requirements in the area of switching systems e.g. real time constraints and concurrency are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Representation of security policy for a telecommunications application
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: A discussion is given on the nature of a security policy and a distinction is made between the concepts of an organisational security policy and an automated security policy. An organisational security policy is the set of laws, rules and practices that regulate how an organisation manages, protects, and distributes resources in order to achieve specified security objectives. An automated security policy is the set of restrictions and properties that specify how a computing system prevents information and computing resources from being (mis)used to violate an organisational security policy. The authors show how to represent organisational policies in terms of an enterprise model, and how restrictions and properties of the automated policy play a key role in the enforcement of the organisational policy. They also present an example showing how these ideas are applied to security policy issues surrounding the automation of an authorisation function for a telecommunications application.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Intelligent networks: computer aided analysis for SLP specification
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The author describes the environment within which an SLP (service logic program) operates, and in particular describes the relationship between SLPs and FCs (functional components). This is followed by a discussion of how the specification of SLPs can be expressed in SDL, which in turn is followed by a brief review of how SLP specifications can be analysed for logical errors based upon SDL dynamic semantics. Then follows a discussion of how specification written in SDL can be analysed for logical errors within an SLP environment, where the errors themselves are defined in SDL. And finally advantages and limitations of the technique are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Formal specification and design of intelligent network services
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: With the introduction of intelligent networks (IN) which will eventually allow service subscribers and network operators to introduce (develop and create) new services directly into the network, it is necessary to provide preventative measures to avoid introducing problems into the network along with the new services. One of such measures is through the use of formal methods to specify and design IN services. Formal methods allow unambiguous specification and formal analysis (and verification) of services and service elements. This is particularly important considering for instance, a set of functional components (FC) that may be used by a number of parties and therefore the interpretation of the 'meaning and behaviour' of the FCs should be precise and accurate. This is particularly so if some FCs are eventually going to be standardised and used as 'off the shelf' basic building blocks for creating new services. Moreover, without formally specifying services and service elements, it will be very difficult, if not impossible, to prove or verify the correctness of the design as well as analysing other properties of services such as features interaction. This paper presents a service specification and design methodology and describes the use of LOTOS as a formal model to represent services.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Network management system graphical interface
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The description of a graphical user interface is presented. This interface is used to construct and manage graphical entities representing telecommunications network objects. Based on the X Windows System version 11 standard, the network management system graphical interface allows the user to build his own window environment on the controlled system through an interactive editor using OSF/Motif toolkit. All events of the controlled network are monitored modifying graphical attributes of objects on the screen. The network management system graphical interface runs on a Unix based graphical workstation which is connected to the controlled system through a host computer, via an Ethernet LAN, using a TCP/IP protocol.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: TROPICO RA O&M development environment
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The TELEBRAS Research & Development Center (CPqD-Telebras) has been developing the TROPICO RA System since 1986. TROPICO is a large SPC telephone exchange, the evolution of which has been divided into a series of phases. From the source system, it is possible to produce different equipment configurations whose capacity ranges from hundreds to tens of thousand of subscribers. The technologies used during the TROPICO RA development have been created in CPqD with the main purpose of rationalizing the system development life cycle. The Sysware Technology (P.A. Mannby, 1988), is a guide to the system functional design where the system functions to be provided are identified and described. These include the operational and maintenance (O&M) functions. The O&Mware technology, also used during the functional design phase, aids the designers to describe the O&M functions. All the functions conceived and described are later implemented using the TROPICO software or hardware technology. In order to support these technologies an integrated system development environment was specially conceived. The O&M development environment is part of this integrated environment and backs up the O&Mware technology.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Multi-thread interface for telecommunications applications
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: Telecommunications applications offer one of the most challenging domains for applications-interfaces. This paper presents an application-interface which adopts a flexible approach to the presentation of information and handles multiple access for different types of users. The work is funded by British Telecom as part of a project focusing on distributed resource allocation within a dynamic environment. In the next decade, the development of telecommunications services will generate a new technological revolution from which massive financial and employment benefits are expected. Private networks will play a vital role in the management of companies and the public will have access to a multitude of new services. Application-interfaces will have a vital part to play in achieving this revolution; by providing users (e.g: managers, field staff, customers) with access to a wide range of management facilities.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A software toolkit for network and service planning
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: Planning the evolution of a large telecommunication networks is a difficult task. Using a software tools approach to improve the network and service planning process, the authors have realized the benefits of performance planning through the application of graphics and object-oriented database technology to manipulate network data and facilitate decision making. A software toolkit has been built to allow a user to interact with a comprehensive model of the AT&T telecommunications network to evaluate network performance from an individual service or customer perspective. This toolkit includes powerful and flexible network querying capability to map from physical network components to logical services, customized network graphics, traditional software productivity tools (spreadsheets, SQL queries), and a plug-in interface to numerical analysis modules. Using this toolkit, the network manager can quickly identify potential trouble areas in the network, quantify the impact of network failures in terms of individual service and customer performance, formulate strategies to improve the performance, and evaluate the end results of implementing various plans.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An integrated software engineering environment: a semantic view
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: This paper presents a workstation-based, integrated software engineering environment for control-oriented telecommunication software. Emphasis is placed on the semantic aspects of integration and the subject is considered from a user requirements perspective. It is shown how highly effective integration can be achieved with little modification to existing tools using ARCADE, a set of integration facilities at the presentation and process level. An important characteristic of the environment is the separation between integration facilities and the object management system. The approach is shown to be complementary to one based on a message communication facility.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimisation strategies and performance evaluation of the two-phase commit protocol
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: A discussion is given on some optimization strategies and performance evaluations of the two-phase commit protocol, which insures, even in case of failures, the atomicity of updates executed on different sites by a distributed transaction. The performance evaluations have been realized by simulation runs using the queueing network tool QNAP2 from INRIA/Simulog and compared with theoretical costs. This study has been performed in the context of INRIA involvement in ISO WG5 work on OSI-TP.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Broadband multi-service networks-the software challenge
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The authors review some of the services that could be supported over a broadband multi-service network and present some of the associated control and management issues. The wide range of services which need to be supported will challenge the design of the associated software system. A number of standards have and are being developed to help with this and there are many exciting issues to be addressed on the route to a broadband multi-service network. By drawing on practical work currently being undertaken within BT Laboratories and studies into available equipment, a progression from MAN systems, initially supporting only a few services, to a broadband multi-service network, is presented as the likely evolutionary path. The authors raise the question as to whether a software system can be flexible, service independent, fast, reliable, and at the same time remain cost effective.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An entity-based service script editor for IN
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The Intelligent Network (IN) concepts have a very simple objective: to allow innovative telecommunications services to be delivered quickly to end users. While there are several IN systems available today, they are really just a first step towards the overall objective. There are several areas which need to be clarified before full-specification systems can be developed, one of which is service creation (SC). The overall strategy on SC is clear: the best way to speed up software production for services is to encapsulate the capabilities of the network as an extensible set of standard building blocks, from which new services can be created at a high level of abstraction. This can perhaps be likened to the 'fourth generation language' approach to writing database queries. The authors' work on the editing of service logic programs (SLPs), or 'scripts', is targeted at the high-level, user-oriented style of description. This complements the more 'bottom-up' approach of existing analyses such as the CCITT work on service independent building blocks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An implementation of object modelled network management
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The software industry is a minefield. It is littered with dangerous technological fads, waiting to blow up your project. The authors present an object modelled network management project which made it through the minefield. The management system (MS) runs on personal computers. It is aimed, with an attractive price, at small to medium sized networks. Despite this it offers very advanced functionality and incorporates open systems interconnection (OSI) communications technology. The authors describe the functionality of the system, interesting aspects of the design and the story of the project. They specifically discuss the following topics: functions of the system, design features, control of requirements, quality control, project management and cost control.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A bridge from structured analysis (SA/RT) to specification and description language (SDL)
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: A new method for transformation from SA/RT to SDL has been developed. The method consists of a hybrid modelling language, serving as a bridge between the two expression techniques, together with a set of transformation rules and guidelines. This paper shows how SA/RT can serve as a front-end extension to SDL and that a rule based transformation is both feasible and practical.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Process algebra techniques for verification of SDL-diagrams
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The authors show how techniques from process algebra can be profitably applied to verification of SDL-diagrams stemming from real life applications in the area of communication protocols. The advantage gained is a speed-up of the development cycle. Instead of searching for errors in the testing phase only the authors' verification aims at the design phase and thus cuts short the development cycle. A second advantage is higher confidence in the correctness of the system. They assume that the design is made by means of diagrams of the CCITT language SDL (specification and description language). The authors believe that only on the design level the systems are sufficiently abstract and concise to be amenable to formal verification.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Service description and implementation based on the connection-oriented model
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: This paper describes a connection-oriented model for the description of multi-party, multi-connection services at different abstraction levels. The transformation between two levels is illustrated by means of a supplementary service example. The model has been prototyped using the object-oriented knowledge base system KIWIS.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Methods for service software design
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: The need to define an appropriate software support was recognised within the European RACE I programme, and a group of four projects have contributed to a programming infrastructure (PI). Within the PI the Specification and Programming Environment for Communications Systems (SPECS) project has a primary aim to specify a methodology to provide maximum automation and optimization of software engineering of IBC (integrated broadband communication) software from requirements and specification through design, implementation, test, execution, maintenance and adaptation. The project demonstrates how the objective can be achieved by methods using both formal techniques, informal descriptions and engineering judgement. The architecture and tools are outlined in this paper to present a review of SPECS. This paper gives more detail of PEGS methods for elaborating requirements (and existing designs) towards design oriented definitions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Designing the databases of the intelligent network
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: A discussion is given on a distributed database application within an intelligent network in some detail, and identifiers and specific type of distributed database system being dealt with. She continues then into illustrating the types of demands which are going to be placed on the IN in its future development. Partial replication is clearly the better type of replication scheme to handle the demands of the IN but its use is inhibited by two factors, those of the method to be used to locate data in the system and the method to be used to update data. Neither of these problems yet have adequate solutions. Future research in this area of the IN should aim towards developing a concurrency and replication control algorithm which suitably updates the data in the system, and a system catalogue which quickly and accurately locates information of the required consistency in the system. These are current active distributed database research areas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experiences of implementation using advanced intelligent network release 1 architecture
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: Logica Space and Communications Ltd., as sub-contractors to ICL Data Finland are implementing the SCP and SMS part of intelligent network services for Telecom Finland. The IN system will comprise new generation Nokia DX200 digital exchanges, from Nokia Telecommunications, acting as SSP, together with Tandem service control points (SCPs) and service management system (SMS). The architecture used is in accordance with the Bellcore advanced intelligent network, (AIN) release 1 architecture. The system for Telecom Finland is believed to be the first of its kind in the world (using the AIN release 1 architecture), and is expected to be operational by the end of 1992. In the course of the design and implementation, a number of architectural issues have been identified. From his experience in using the new AIN architecture, the author describes some key issues and the solutions that have been adopted. These are: feature interaction rules to cater for when more than one IN feature is invoked for the same call; IN features which continue for an extended period; provision of mechanisms to allow the caller to interrupt the progress of a call-recall facility; and database integrity over multiple SCPs when updates are made directly at an SCP such as for a 'follow-me' service.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Processing ASN.1 specifications in a declarative language
publicationTitle: Eighth International Conference on Software Engineering for Telecommunication Systems and Services, 1992.
abstract: Abstract Syntax Notation One ASN.1 is becoming widely used for the specification of CCITT communication protocols. The purpose of ASN.1 is to have a standardized language to express types with and to have a standardized set of rules to transform an instance of one type into a stream of bytes. This stream of bytes can then be sent on a communication channel set up by the lower layers in the stack of communication protocols, e.g. TCP/IP. This way two different applications written in two completely different languages running on different computers with different internal representation of data can exchange instances of structured data types instead of exchanging bytes or even worse bits. This frees the programmer of a great deal of work, since no code has to be written to process the transport format of the data. This paper describes a compiler which is directed towards the declarative language Erlang. In order to use this compiler, familiarity with the language Erlang is essential.
